chronology.event: One Energy petitioned the Hancock County Commissioners to rename Township Road 215 "Electric Avenue." Without convening a public meeting, the Board decided to attend the Commissioners' daytime meeting and oppose the renaming. At its own regular meeting that evening, residents raised zoning as a way to regulate wind-turbine expansion; counsel explained the R.C. 519.04 steps. After the meeting adjourned, some members stayed to discuss who might serve on a zoning commission and what traits were desirable.
Notice published in the Findlay Courier of a December 20 special meeting listing "two resolutions (zoning and marijuana)."
At the special meeting the Board moved to proceed with zoning and to establish a zoning commission under R.C. 519.04. Both resolutions passed without discussion; public comment was not solicited.
One Energy filed case 2024 CV 00038 seeking declaratory relief for Open Meetings Act violations.

The Board adopted a revised notice policy (fearing the original rule was lost or destroyed) and RESCINDED both December 20 zoning resolutions. Minutes reflect the township attorney recommending that residents be required to petition for zoning.
Hancock County Board of Elections certified the resident petitions.
Nine petitions bearing 141 signatures were presented, asking the Board to move to place zoning for the unincorporated areas on the ballot. The Board instructed the attorney to prepare a resolution.
A protest was filed against the Board of Elections' certification placing zoning on the November ballot.

After an eight-minute executive session on pending litigation, the Board proceeded with zoning BY ITS OWN RESOLUTION rather than on the petitions, and passed a second resolution establishing a new zoning commission. The new commission's members gathered afterward; One Energy's president/CEO claimed his filming was thwarted.

One Energy filed a second complaint (the opinion writes "2024-CR-161" here; the caption page says 2024 CV 00161) alleging the Board failed to deliberate in public over who would sit on the zoning commission and by what criteria.
Trial. One Energy expressly disclaimed statutory damages, attorney's fees and costs, seeking only compliance, declarations, and invalidation of the April 2024 zoning commission.
Final judgment entries in both cases.

violations_found:
Taking an official position opposing the renaming of Township Road 215 without discussing it in an open meeting violated R.C. 121.22. The chairman testified he discussed the position by phone with the other members and then stated "the Board's position" at the Commissioners' meeting (¶29). Pleading objection rejected: Ohio is a notice-pleading state and the issue was fully litigated (¶27).
Remaining after the December 5, 2023 meeting to discuss criteria for selecting zoning commission members was a deliberation, not fact-finding, and violated the Act (¶¶33-34).
claims_rejected: Notice of the December 20, 2023 special meeting was sufficient.
The December 5, 2023 minutes were prepared in a timely manner.
The April 2, 2024 executive session was properly invoked to discuss the One Energy litigation.
The evidence did not establish that the decision to proceed with zoning resulted from nonpublic deliberations.

remedy.granted: A prospective injunction: the trustees "are prospectively enjoined from engaging in private discussions of public matters in derogation of R.C. §121.22." Mandatory under R.C. 121.22(I)(1) once a violation is proven, though the trial court retains discretion over its terms (¶¶35, 40).
remedy.refused: The court declined to strike the selection criteria or invalidate the April 2024 zoning commission, on the trial court's three stated grounds: the informal discussion produced no official action subject to invalidation; the rescission of the December 2023 resolutions "constitutes an intervening circumstances that breaks any causal link"; and the criteria "were not unique" — "This Court declines to enjoin the use of common sense" (¶40).

holdings.bottom_line: [verified] Both sides lost every assignment of error. The zoning-commission actions of April 2, 2024 STAND. The Open Meetings Act violations are real and declared, but they did not undo the zoning track — which is why the instrument that eventually reached the electorate traces to the April 2024 resolution and not to the rescinded December 2023 one.

key_authority: Look Ahead Am. v. Stark Cnty. Bd. of Elections, 2024-Ohio-2691, ¶15 — OMA interpretation is de novo
State ex rel. Pelmear v. Henry Cnty. Land Reutilization Corp., 2025-Ohio-4998, ¶24, ¶30
Ames v. Rootstown Twp. Bd. of Trustees, 2022-Ohio-4605, ¶¶20-21 — injunction mandatory, terms discretionary
State ex rel. Bratenahl v. Village of Bratenahl, 2019-Ohio-3233, ¶23 — rescission does not moot a proven violation
Springfield Local Sch. Dist. Bd. of Educ. v. Ohio Assn. of Pub. Sch. Emps., Local 530, 106 Ohio App.3d 855 (9th Dist.) — causation required beyond the act of deliberation
Blakemore v. Blakemore, 5 Ohio St.3d 217, 219 (1983) — abuse-of-discretion standard

corroboration.claim: The Wind-for-Industry turbines serve industrial hosts, not the Megawatt Hub.
corroboration.detail: ¶2 of the opinion states as the court's own background that One Energy "was making plans to construct additional wind turbines in Allen Township to, inter alia, provide power to the Whirlpool manufacturing facility." Independently corroborates the correction recorded in issue 1464 (see data/extracted/grid/findlay/) that nothing places generation at the Megawatt Hub, from a source that is neither a company filing nor press.

corroboration.claim: The zoning fight was triggered by WIND, and data centers were nowhere in it.
corroboration.detail: The opinion's entire factual account — turbines, a road renaming, a zoning commission — runs from late 2023 through December 2024 without a single reference to data centers or computing load. The data-center question arrives in Allen Township only in 2026, after the resolution is already adopted and awaiting a referendum. That sequencing is why the adopted resolution has no data-center provision to be found: it was not drafted against that use.

corrections_to_issue_body:
The issue body compresses "resident petitions (141 signatures, BOE-certified 2024-02-26)" into the causal chain, but ¶13 is explicit that the Board did NOT proceed on the petitions: "Despite the petitions that had been submitted, the Board elected to proceed with zoning through their own resolution." The petitions were certified and presented; the trustees then used their own R.C. 519 track instead.
The issue body gives no appellate case numbers. They are 5-25-02 and 5-25-03 — two consolidated appeals, one per trial-court case.
The issue body says the trial court found "limited violations ... but the zoning-commission actions stand." Accurate, and now sourced: ¶19 quotes the entry directly, and ¶¶40-46 give the three reasons the commission survived.

The two Common Pleas judgment entries themselves (2024 CV 00038 Doc. No. 79; 2024 CV 00161 Doc. No. 66) — quoted in the opinion but not held. The Clerk of Courts eServices portal timed out on capture; see the access_failures block in the governance filename-map.

The identities of the co-plaintiff "entities that have land interests in Allen Township" (fn.1). Relevant to any vested-rights claim over the Megawatt Hub parcels.

Whether the 2024-01-11 Review Plan signals a RENEWED/active federal feasibility effort or is an archival closeout is an [inference] from the document type (a Review Plan is USACE QA/peer-review scoping, normally produced at the START of a feasibility study) and its title ("Feasibility Study of flood risk management and ecosystem restorations plans"). The 2015 USACE recommended plan ("Western Diversion of Eagle Creek") is characterized as having a NEGATIVE benefit-cost ratio in the program FAQ, but no NUMERIC 2015 BCR is public in any source reached. warnings: The 3.2 metric tons (Table A4.1) and the 3,200 kg (OHP000001 Part IV.A.1) are the SAME allocation stated in two units by two instruments, not two allocations. Do not add them.

Table A4.5's seven numeric columns are, in order, 2008 / WLA / 2017 / 2018 / 2019 / 2020 / 2021. The first column is a 2008 baseline load and the second is the allocation — reading the row left-to-right as a time series would misreport both.

The most recent per-facility spring load on this record is 2021. The 2024 Biennial Report publishes only the BASIN GROUP total, not Findlay's own load, so no post-2021 Findlay figure is asserted here. Whether Findlay is still over its allocation is [open] — the annual Season Report required by OHP000001 Part IV.D is the record that would answer it (a records-request lead).

fields.note: [verified] Findlay WPCF's spring-season total-phosphorus wasteload allocation is 3.2 metric tons (3,200 kg), and its reported spring loads for every year on the TMDL's own record — 2017 through 2021 — were 4.8, 5.5, 5.3, 5.5 and 5.4 metric tons. Its 2008 baseline load, 4.4 MT, was also above it. The allocation is enforced not through the plant's individual permit but through the Maumee Watershed Total Phosphorus general permit OHP000001, whose compliance rule (Part IV.C.3) makes an individual exceedance a violation ONLY when the 39-facility CUMULATIVE load also exceeds its cap. In the 2024 spring season the group reported 43,304 kg against a 64,170 kg cap — 20,866 kg of headroom — so an over-allocation Findlay load was not, on that record, a violation of anything.
